Differentially Private GraphRAG: Protecting Relation Connectivity and Semantics

Conference: ; ;
Jie Fu Affiliation: Stevens Institute of Technology, Hoboken, NJ, USA email: jfu13@stevens.edu , Yuan Hong Affiliation: University of Connecticut, Storrs, CT, USA email: yuan.hong@uconn.edu , Yue Ning Affiliation: Stevens Institute of Technology, Hoboken, NJ, USA email: Yue.Ning@stevens.edu and Wendy Hui Wang Affiliation: Stevens Institute of Technology, Hoboken, NJ, USA email: hwang4@stevens.edu
© none
Abstract.

Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) connects information across documents through entity relationships to support relational reasoning. However, black-box access to GraphRAG systems can enable adversaries to reconstruct knowledge graphs and recover both structural connectivity between entities and the semantics of their relationships. Existing defenses lack formal privacy guarantees and provide limited protection against such reconstruction attacks. We propose RelGuard, the first differentially private framework for GraphRAG, which provides formal privacy guarantees by mitigating connectivity leakage and protecting relations and their semantic meaning through relation removal. We formalize relation differential privacy (relation-DP), which bounds the distinguishability of mechanism outputs according to the semantic distance between alternative relations while accounting for relation removal. Building on this definition, we develop a four-step defense mechanism that sanitizes source documents before GraphRAG indexing by perturbing relation predicates or removing their associated connectivity using the exponential mechanism. Experiments across three GraphRAG systems and two targeted reconstruction attacks demonstrate that RelGuard provides stronger protection against reconstruction attacks than four existing defense mechanisms while better preserving downstream utility.

Keywords: 
GraphRAG, Differential Privacy, Relation Privacy Protection

1. Introduction

Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) integrates knowledge graphs, which represent entities and their relationships, with unstructured text corpora to support knowledge retrieval, domain-specific question answering, and multi-hop reasoning in Web services (Edge et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). By modeling relationships among entities, GraphRAG enables information scattered across documents to be connected and retrieved through graph structures, enhancing the relational reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs).

However, the relational information that enables these capabilities also creates privacy risks. We consider two complementary dimensions of relation privacy: (1) structural connectivity, which reveals whether two entities are connected in the knowledge graph, and (2) relation semantics, which reveals the nature of the relationship between connected entities. An adversary who infers connectivity can discover previously unknown associations between entities, while recovering relation semantics can further reveal the specific nature of those associations. Recent studies have demonstrated that adversaries can recover such information by reconstructing knowledge graphs through black-box access to GraphRAG systems (Liu et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026; Song et al., 2026). Although existing defense mechanisms attempt to mitigate these reconstruction attacks (Gu et al., 2026; Song et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2024), they lack formal privacy guarantees, leaving the extent of information leakage difficult to characterize and control.

To address this limitation, we propose RelGuard, the first differentially private framework for GraphRAG, protecting relation semantics while mitigating connectivity leakage. Our key insight is that relation protection must account for both the existence of a relationship and its meaning when present. Simply suppressing edges can protect connectivity but may unnecessarily impair downstream reasoning, whereas replacing relation predicates without accounting for edge removal does not provide a unified treatment of both privacy dimensions.

First, we formalize relation differential privacy (relation-DP), a metric-based privacy definition that calibrates output indistinguishability to the semantic distance between alternative relation predicates while also accounting for the possibility of relation removal. This formulation bounds the distinguishability of released relation semantics, while relation removal helps protect connectivity.

Second, we develop a four-step defense mechanism that sanitizes private documents before they are indexed by GraphRAG. Specifically, RelGuard: (1) extracts canonical entity–relation triples from the private documents; (2) generates candidate relation predicates for each extracted relation; (3) perturbs each relation by sampling a replacement predicate or a null outcome, which suppresses the corresponding connectivity; and (4) reconstructs sanitized documents by consistently updating relation expressions or removing sentences associated with null outcomes. GraphRAG then builds its index from the sanitized documents and uses the resulting index for query answering. This design integrates formal relation privacy protection into the GraphRAG pipeline while seeking to preserve the information needed for accurate question answering.

We evaluate RelGuard on three GraphRAG systems and two real-world datasets, comparing it against four existing defense mechanisms. RelGuard achieves the lowest relation recovery F1 across all the settings and the lowest connection recovery F1 in most settings. In particular, it reduces relation recovery F1 by 26.98%–44.35% compared with the strongest baseline. Meanwhile, RelGuard achieves the best privacy–utility trade-off, limiting the reduction in question-answering F1 to just 2.98%–8.97%. These results demonstrate that RelGuard provides stronger protection against relation reconstruction while preserving high utility for downstream question answering.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

  • ∙\bullet

    We introduce relation differential privacy (relation-DP), a metric-based privacy framework for formally protecting relation semantics and mitigating connectivity leakage in GraphRAG.

  • ∙\bullet

    We design a relation-DP-based defense mechanism that sanitizes source documents before GraphRAG indexing, jointly protecting relation semantics and connectivity through relation substitution and removal.

  • ∙\bullet

    Our extensive empirical evaluation demonstrates the advantages of RelGuard over existing defenses in terms of both privacy protection and utility preservation.

2. Background

2.1. Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) uses graph-structured knowledge to retrieve connected evidence for LLM generation (Edge et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). Systems either retrieve from existing knowledge graphs or construct graph indexes from documents (Peng et al., 2025). We focus on document-based GraphRAG, which extracts entities and relations from source text and retains associated passages as evidence.

Index construction. Given a private document DD, the system constructs an index ℐ=𝖨𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗑⁡(D)\mathcal{I}=\mathsf{Index}(D) containing a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E). Each triple (s,r,o)(s,r,o) represents a relation rr from subject entity ss to object entity oo. The index may also store source passages, entity and relation descriptions, community summaries, and vector representations (Edge et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025).

Retrieval and generation. For a query qq, the retriever selects evidence Cq=𝖱𝖾𝗍𝗋𝗂𝖾𝗏𝖾⁡(q,ℐ)C_{q}=\mathsf{Retrieve}(q,\mathcal{I}), which the LLM uses to generate an answer y^=𝖦𝖾𝗇𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗍𝖾⁡(q,Cq)\widehat{y}=\mathsf{Generate}(q,C_{q}). LightRAG uses dual-level retrieval (Guo et al., 2025), PathRAG retrieves relational paths (Chen et al., 2026), and HippoRAG 2 uses associative retrieval (Gutiérrez et al., 2025). Retrieved evidence can include both graph relationships and associated text.

2.2. Differential Privacy

Differential privacy (DP) bounds how much the output distribution of a randomized mechanism can change when its protected input changes (Dwork et al., 2006; Dwork and Roth, 2014).

Definition 1 (ϵ\epsilon-Differential Privacy).

Let x∼x′x\sim x^{\prime} denote neighboring inputs differing in one protected unit. A randomized mechanism ℳ:𝒳→𝒴\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Y} satisfies ϵ\epsilon-DP if, for every neighboring pair and every measurable output event 𝒮⊆𝒴\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{Y},

(1) Pr[ℳ(x)∈𝒮]≤eϵPr[ℳ(x′)∈𝒮].\Pr[\mathcal{M}(x)\in\mathcal{S}]\leq e^{\epsilon}\Pr[\mathcal{M}(x^{\prime})\in\mathcal{S}].

Smaller ϵ\epsilon imposes a tighter bound on distinguishability. Standard DP specifies protected comparisons through binary adjacency. Metric-DP instead uses an input distance to express how the privacy bound varies across possible values (Chatzikokolakis et al., 2013; Fernandes et al., 2019).

Definition 2 (ϵ\epsilon-Metric Differential Privacy).

For a metric space (𝒳,d𝒳)(\mathcal{X},d_{\mathcal{X}}), a randomized mechanism ℳ\mathcal{M} satisfies ϵ\epsilon-metric-DP if, for every x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X} and measurable output event 𝒮\mathcal{S},

(2) Pr[ℳ(x)∈𝒮]≤eϵ​d𝒳​(x,x′)Pr[ℳ(x′)∈𝒮].\Pr[\mathcal{M}(x)\in\mathcal{S}]\leq e^{\epsilon d_{\mathcal{X}}(x,x^{\prime})}\Pr[\mathcal{M}(x^{\prime})\in\mathcal{S}].

The input distance d𝒳d_{\mathcal{X}} in ϵ\epsilon-metric-DP must satisfy the triangle inequality: d𝒳​(x,z)≤d𝒳​(x,x′)+d𝒳​(x′,z)d_{\mathcal{X}}(x,z)\leq d_{\mathcal{X}}(x,x^{\prime})+d_{\mathcal{X}}(x^{\prime},z) for all x,x′,z∈𝒳x,x^{\prime},z\in\mathcal{X}. Nearby inputs receive a tighter bound; more distant inputs permit larger differences between output distributions. Metric-DP captures semantic differences through input distances. Text-privacy methods use Euclidean distance between word embeddings (Feyisetan et al., 2020), Mahalanobis distance in sentence-embedding space (Bollegala et al., 2025), and Earth Mover’s distance between bags of word embeddings (Fernandes et al., 2019). The metric and its scale must be specified together with ϵ\epsilon.

A common approach to achieving ϵ\epsilon-metric-DP is the exponential mechanism, which selects from a finite candidate set according to a utility score (McSherry and Talwar, 2007; Chatzikokolakis et al., 2013). Let x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} be the private input, 𝒴\mathcal{Y} a fixed finite output set, and u:𝒳×𝒴→ℝu:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} a utility function satisfying

|u⁡(x,y)−u⁡(x′,y)|≤d𝒳​(x,x′)|u(x,y)-u(x^{\prime},y)|\leq d_{\mathcal{X}}(x,x^{\prime})

for all x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X} and y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. Sampling according to

(3) Pr[ℳEM(x)=y]=exp⁡(ϵ​u​(x,y)/2)∑z∈𝒴exp⁡(ϵ​u​(x,z)/2)\Pr[\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{EM}}(x)=y]=\frac{\exp(\epsilon u(x,y)/2)}{\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Y}}\exp(\epsilon u(x,z)/2)}

satisfies ϵ\epsilon-metric-DP. Higher-utility candidates are more likely, with ϵ\epsilon controlling concentration.

3. Related Work

Privacy inference in GraphRAG. RAG systems are vulnerable to text extraction (Cohen et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024) and membership inference (Li et al., 2025). GraphRAG attacks further recover entity connections and relation semantics from generated answers. Untargeted attacks seek broad graph recovery: AGEA uses graph memory and novelty-guided exploration (Yang et al., 2026), while GraphSteal expands entity neighborhoods through breadth-wise traversal (Gu et al., 2026). Targeted attacks recover relations around a specified entity. GraphSteal uses depth-wise search, whereas GRASP frames extraction as structured relation processing with record identifiers and adaptive queries (Song et al., 2026). We evaluate both connection and semantic relation recovery under targeted attacks.

Privacy defenses for GraphRAG. Existing defenses modify generation instructions or retrieved contexts. Protective Prompt restricts disclosure of retrieved content (Gu et al., 2026), while Abstractive requires query-relevant paraphrasing (Liu et al., 2026; Song et al., 2026). GRASP’s ID Alignment collapses record identifiers, and Decoy adds misleading endpoint fields to disrupt structured extraction (Song et al., 2026). These defenses aim to reduce extraction but provide no formal privacy guarantees. In contrast, our framework provides relation-DP guarantees through document sanitization before indexing.

Metric-DP on text. Prior work applies metric-DP to word embeddings (Feyisetan et al., 2020), sentence representations (Bollegala et al., 2025), and LLM-generated substitutes (Awon et al., 2025). Prϵ​ϵ\epsilon\epsilonmpt combines metric-DP with format-preserving encryption for sensitive prompt values (Chowdhury et al., 2025), while TDP substitutes sensitive entities in LLM contexts (Yu et al., 2026). These methods protect textual units rather than explicitly addressing both the semantics and existence of relationships between entities. Our framework targets relation-level privacy, combining semantic replacement and relation deletion to protect relation meaning and mitigate connectivity leakage.

4. Problem Setup

4.1. Semantic Distance between Relations

We define an embedding-based semantic distance between relation predicates for the privacy guarantee in Section 4.2. We also describe the extension used to represent connectivity perturbation.

Distance between predicates. Let ℛ\mathcal{R} denote the domain of relations, and let Emb:ℛ→ℝp\operatorname{Emb}:\mathcal{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{p} be a fixed encoder that maps each relation to a finite, nonzero embedding vector (Ushio et al., 2021; Gábor et al., 2017). For each r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}, we define its normalized embedding as

(4) z⁡(r)=Emb⁡(r)‖Emb⁡(r)‖2.z(r)=\frac{\operatorname{Emb}(r)}{\|\operatorname{Emb}(r)\|_{2}}.

The semantic distance between two predicates r,r′∈ℛr,r^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} is defined as

(5) dℛ​(r,r′)=12​‖z⁡(r)−z⁡(r′)‖2.d_{\mathcal{R}}(r,r^{\prime})=\frac{1}{2}\|z(r)-z(r^{\prime})\|_{2}.

Since the embeddings are unit-normalized, this distance depends only on their directions and is independent of their magnitudes. Furthermore, dℛ​(r,r′)∈[0,1]d_{\mathcal{R}}(r,r^{\prime})\in[0,1], with smaller values indicating greater embedding-based semantic similarity and larger values indicating greater semantic dissimilarity. The scaled Euclidean distance satisfies the triangle inequality, as shown in Appendix A.1. It is a metric when r↦z⁡(r)r\mapsto z(r) is injective and otherwise a pseudometric; the privacy proof covers both cases.

Extended distance between triples under connectivity perturbation. In addition to perturbing relation semantics, our defense may remove edges from the relation graph to protect connectivity privacy. To capture such structural perturbation, we introduce a special marker null to represent the absence of an edge between the subject ss and object oo. Specifically, for a triple t=(s,r,o)t=(s,r,o) and its edge-removed counterpart t′=(s,null,o)t^{\prime}=(s,\texttt{null},o), we define their distance as

(6) d𝒯​(t,t′)=λ,λ>0,d_{\mathcal{T}}(t,t^{\prime})=\lambda,\qquad\lambda>0,

where λ\lambda is a predefined positive constant that quantifies the distance associated with connectivity perturbation. We assign a constant distance λ\lambda because it separates the cost of structural changes from semantic differences and provides a uniform measure of the privacy cost associated with removing any edge. The value of λ\lambda controls the relative distance assigned to edge removal compared with relation substitution and is fixed across all relations to ensure a consistent distance definition.

4.2. Relation Differential Privacy

While conventional DP (Dwork et al., 2006; Dwork and Roth, 2014) provides a rigorous framework for limiting the information revealed about private data, its standard formulation typically assigns the same privacy bound to all neighboring inputs. This uniform treatment does not distinguish between relation substitutions that preserve similar semantics and those that substantially change the meaning of a knowledge graph fact. On the other hand, metric-DP generalizes conventional DP by incorporating a distance function over inputs, allowing the privacy guarantee to vary with the distance between them. Motivated by this flexibility, we introduce relation differential privacy (relation-DP), which instantiates the metric-DP principle for relations by defining privacy in terms of semantic distances between relations.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} denote the domain of relation predicates, and let 𝒪=ℛ∪{null}\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{R}\cup\{\texttt{null}\} be the output space, where null is a special marker indicating the absence of an edge. We define ϵ\epsilon-Relation Differential Privacy as follows.

Definition 1 (ϵ\epsilon-Relation Differential Privacy).

A randomized mechanism ℳ:ℛ→𝒪\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{R}\to\mathcal{O} satisfies ϵ\epsilon-relation-DP if, for every pair of input relations r,r′∈ℛr,r^{\prime}\in\mathcal{R} and every output event 𝒮⊆𝒪\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{O},

(7) Pr[ℳ(r)∈𝒮]≤eϵ​dℛ​(r,r′)Pr[ℳ(r′)∈𝒮],\Pr[\mathcal{M}(r)\in\mathcal{S}]\leq e^{\epsilon d_{\mathcal{R}}(r,r^{\prime})}\Pr[\mathcal{M}(r^{\prime})\in\mathcal{S}],

where dℛd_{\mathcal{R}} is the relation distance defined in Eq. (5).

Relation-DP bounds the distinguishability of both released predicates and retention or deletion outcomes under alternative predicates on a fixed entity pair. The guarantee provides tighter indistinguishability bounds for semantically closer input relations and correspondingly weaker bounds for more distant relations.

Document-level extension. We extend ϵ\epsilon-relation-DP from individual relations to the collection of relations extracted from a document. Let DD and D′D^{\prime} be two private documents, and let ℱ⁡(D)=(ti)i=1m\mathcal{F}(D)=(t_{i})_{i=1}^{m} and ℱ⁡(D′)=(ti′)i=1m\mathcal{F}(D^{\prime})=(t_{i}^{\prime})_{i=1}^{m} denote their ordered canonical triples, where ti=(si,ri,oi)t_{i}=(s_{i},r_{i},o_{i}) and ti′=(si,ri′,oi)t_{i}^{\prime}=(s_{i},r_{i}^{\prime},o_{i}) for all i∈{1,…,m}i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}. We compare documents that differ only in the protected relation expressions, with all remaining text and occurrence mappings unchanged. We define the distance between the two collections of triples as the sum of the distances between their corresponding relations:

(8) dℱ​(ℱ⁡(D),ℱ⁡(D′))=∑i=1mdℛ​(ri,ri′).d_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}(D),\mathcal{F}(D^{\prime}))=\sum_{i=1}^{m}d_{\mathcal{R}}(r_{i},r_{i}^{\prime}).

Suppose a randomized mechanism independently perturbs each relation using an ϵ\epsilon-relation-DP mechanism and reconstructs the perturbed triples while preserving their subject and object entities. Then, for every such pair D,D′D,D^{\prime} and every joint output event 𝒮\mathcal{S}, the resulting mechanism ℳ\mathcal{M} satisfies

(9) Pr[ℳ(D)∈𝒮]≤eϵ​dℱ​(ℱ⁡(D),ℱ⁡(D′))Pr[ℳ(D′)∈𝒮].\Pr[\mathcal{M}(D)\in\mathcal{S}]\leq e^{\epsilon d_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}(D),\mathcal{F}(D^{\prime}))}\Pr[\mathcal{M}(D^{\prime})\in\mathcal{S}].

Thus, the document-level privacy guarantee follows from the individual relation-DP guarantees through composition, with the overall privacy bound determined by the sum of the distances between corresponding relations. The composition proof is provided in Appendix A.2.

4.3. Threat Model and Defense Goal

Attack goal. Given a private document DD and a target entity stargets_{\text{target}} appearing in it, the adversary aims to infer sensitive information associated with stargets_{\text{target}} from GraphRAG answers. Specifically, the attack targets two types of information:

  • •

    Connectivity leakage: The adversary aims to identify which object entities in DD are directly connected to stargets_{\text{target}}.

  • •

    Relation semantics leakage: The adversary aims to infer the semantic meaning of the relationship between stargets_{\text{target}} and each directly connected object entity. An inference is considered successful if the inferred relation is semantically equivalent to the true relation, even if its exact representation differs.

Adversary capabilities. We consider a strong, knowledge-rich adversary who knows the identities of all object entities appearing in the private document DD, but has no prior knowledge of the relationships among them. This assumption reflects scenarios in which entity identities are publicly available or already known to the adversary. It also establishes a conservative threat model in which privacy protection does not rely on concealing the entity set, but instead focuses on protecting sensitive relationships among known entities.

Although the adversary is strong in terms of prior knowledge, we assume that it interacts with GraphRAG as an external user and therefore has only black-box access to the service. This setting reflects practical deployments in which the underlying document, graph index, retrieved context, and model parameters are not exposed to users. The adversary can submit natural-language queries, observe generated answers, and adapt subsequent queries based on information accumulated from previous responses. However, it cannot directly inspect the private document or the system’s internal components, nor can it modify the document or index. Document poisoning and system compromise are outside our threat model.

Figure 1 illustrates the threat model. Suppose a private document states that Alice works for Company B, where Alice is the target entity stargets_{\text{target}}. The adversary knows the identities of Alice and Company B, as well as all other object entities appearing in the private document, but has no prior knowledge of the relationships among them. Through black-box queries to the GraphRAG system, the adversary may infer whether Alice is connected to Company B and, if so, the semantic meaning of their relationship. For example, an answer describing Alice as an employee of Company B reveals both the Alice--Company B connection and its employment semantics, even without explicitly reproducing the predicate works_for. By issuing adaptive follow-up queries, the adversary may attempt to identify all object entities directly connected to Alice and infer the semantic meaning of each corresponding relationship, thereby reconstructing Alice’s entire one-hop neighborhood.

Defense objective. We aim to design a defense mechanism that mitigates the disclosure of sensitive relations involving stargets_{\text{target}} along two complementary dimensions: structural privacy, which limits the ability to infer whether stargets_{\text{target}} is connected to other entities, and semantic privacy, which limits the ability to infer the meanings of these relations. At the same time, the defense should preserve the utility of the protected document for downstream question answering (QA). To achieve these objectives, we develop a relation-level perturbation mechanism guided by the relation-DP guarantee (Definition 1), with the goal of protecting sensitive relational information while retaining sufficient semantic and structural information for accurate QA.

5. Methodology

Given a private document DD and privacy budget ϵ\epsilon, RelGuard generates a sanitized document D~\widetilde{D} for GraphRAG indexing and query answering. Figure 2 shows four steps: (1) extract canonical entity–relation triples and record their occurrences; (2) generate type-conditioned candidate relations; (3) perturb relations using these candidates and null; and (4) reconstruct D~\widetilde{D} from the perturbed triples. We describe each step below.

5.1. Relation Extraction

The first step of RelGuard is to extract subject–relation–object triples from the private document DD. We use a large language model (LLM) for this task (Huguet Cabot and Navigli, 2021; Mo et al., 2025). The LLM extracts only relations supported by the document, excluding unsupported, negated, or hypothetical relations. The extraction prompt is provided in Appendix B.

To ensure consistent representation, entity aliases and unambiguous coreferential mentions are mapped to the same entity identity, and semantically equivalent relation expressions are normalized into snake_case predicates while preserving subject–object direction. For example, both Alice works at Company B and Alice is employed by Company B are normalized to the same triple, (`​Alice′,works_for,`​Company B′)(`\text{Alice}^{\prime},\texttt{works\_for},`\text{Company B}^{\prime}).

5.2. Relation Candidate Generation

Next, RelGuard generates candidate relations for perturbing each extracted triple. The key idea is to construct candidate pools based on the types of the subject and object entities, rather than the original relation. Specifically, RelGuard follows two steps to generate the candidates: (1) Entity typing: it assigns each entity a type from a fixed inventory; (2) Candidate generation: it generates a pool of candidate predicates for each observed relation based on the types of its subject and object entities. All triples with the same subject and object entities use the same candidate pool. This design makes generated relation candidates independent of the extracted ones and avoids generating a separate pool for every triple. Next, we explain the details of the two steps.

Entity typing. Given the set of canonical entities VV appearing in the extracted triples, we define a type assignment function τ:V→𝒰\tau:V\to\mathcal{U} that assigns each entity a type from a fixed inventory. Specifically, we adopt an entity-type inventory based on OntoNotes (Weischedel et al., 2013):

(10) 𝒰={\displaystyle\mathcal{U}=\{ Person,Norp,Fac,Org,Gpe,Loc,Product,Event,\displaystyle\textsc{Person},\textsc{Norp},\textsc{Fac},\textsc{Org},\textsc{Gpe},\textsc{Loc},\textsc{Product},\textsc{Event},
Work_Of_Art,Law,Language}.\displaystyle\textsc{Work\_Of\_Art},\textsc{Law},\textsc{Language}\}.

Each entity is assigned a type based on its canonical identity and the fixed inventory, without using source sentences or extracted relation predicates. Given a subject entity ss and an object entity oo, we define their ordered type pair as

g⁡(s,o)=(τ⁡(s),τ⁡(o)),g(s,o)=(\tau(s),\tau(o)),

where the subject type always comes first and the object type second. This ordering is essential because relation predicates are directional: reversing the subject and object types can change the set of type-compatible predicates. For example, works_for describes a relation from a person to an organization, whereas employs describes the corresponding relation in the reverse direction. Accordingly, these two directions are treated as distinct type pairs for candidate generation. In our running example, Alice is assigned type Person and Company B type Org, yielding g⁡(Alice,Company B)=(Person,Org)g(\texttt{Alice},\texttt{Company B})=(\textsc{Person},\textsc{Org}).

Candidate generation. For each extracted triple (s,r,o)(s,r,o), we prompt an LLM to generate a pool of KK distinct candidate relations for rr, denoted by 𝒞r={r1,…,rK}\mathcal{C}_{r}=\{r_{1},\ldots,r_{K}\}, where K≥1K\geq 1 is a user-specified parameter. The candidate relations must satisfy the following three requirements.

  1. (1)

    Type compatibility: Each ri∈𝒞rr_{i}\in\mathcal{C}_{r} must represent a plausible relation between entity types τ⁡(s)\tau(s) and τ⁡(o)\tau(o). For example, for the type pair (Person,Org)(\textsc{Person},\textsc{Org}), plausible relations include works_for, founded, and invests_in, whereas headquartered_in is incompatible.

  2. (2)

    Semantic distinctness: The candidate relations must be semantically distinct. Relations that are semantically equivalent, such as synonyms or paraphrases, are merged into a single canonical relation. For example, works_for and employed_by are treated as equivalent, whereas works_for and founded represent distinct relations.

  3. (3)

    Non-subsumption: No candidate relation may subsume another relation in the same pool. If one relation logically implies another, the broader relation is removed in favor of the more specific one. For example, spouse_of implies family_member_of; therefore, the broader family_member_of relation is removed, while the more specific spouse_of relation is retained.

The prompt used for generating candidate relations is provided in Appendix B. Given the generated candidate relations, for each extracted triple t=(s,r,o)t=(s,r,o), we construct its candidate pool (denoted as 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}) as

𝒞t={(s,ri,o)∣ri∈Cr}.\mathcal{C}_{t}=\{(s,r_{i},o)\mid r_{i}\in C_{r}\}.

Thus, all triples sharing the same subject and object entities use the same candidate pool.

5.3. Relation Perturbation

At this stage, RelGuard protects both relation semantics and connectivity by randomly replacing each relation with a candidate from the pool or deleting it. An exponential mechanism governs these choices by balancing semantic preservation against privacy protection through two parameters: ϵ\epsilon, which controls the randomness of the perturbation, and λ\lambda, which controls the propensity for deletion. Algorithm 1 summarizes the relation perturbation procedure. We explain the details below.

For each triple t⁡(s,r,o)t(s,r,o) retrieved from the private document DD, let 𝒞r\mathcal{C}_{r} be its candidate pool (Section 5.2). To perturb both relation meaning and released connectivity, we augment this pool with null: 𝒪r=𝒞r∪{null}\mathcal{O}_{r}=\mathcal{C}_{r}\cup\{\texttt{null}\}. Selecting a real candidate replaces the original relation, whereas selecting null removes the relation from the released representation.

We assign each candidate outcome a utility score based on its semantic distance from the original relation. Specifically, for an original relation rr and a candidate outcome r′∈𝒞rr^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{r}, we define the utility function u⁡(r,r′)u(r,r^{\prime}) for replacing rr with r′r^{\prime} as follows:

(11) u⁡(r,r′)={−dℛ​(r,r′),r′∈𝒞r,−λ,r′=null.u(r,r^{\prime})=\begin{cases}-d_{\mathcal{R}}(r,r^{\prime}),&r^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}_{r},\\ -\lambda,&r^{\prime}=\texttt{null}.\end{cases}

where dℛd_{\mathcal{R}} is defined in Eq. (5) and λ\lambda is defined in Eq. (6).

For a real candidate, the utility is the negative semantic distance, so candidates that preserve more of the original relation’s meaning receive higher scores. In contrast, null represents deletion and has no predicate semantics; we therefore assign it the constant utility −λ-\lambda, independent of the input relation.

The removal distance λ\lambda is fixed across compared inputs but remains a configurable parameter. For a fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and candidate pool, decreasing λ\lambda increases the probability of selecting null, allowing more relations to be removed. This parameter therefore controls the trade-off between privacy protection and question-answering (QA) utility, which we investigate in Section 6.4.

For each relation rr, we independently sample a perturbed outcome r~∈𝒪i\widetilde{r}\in\mathcal{O}_{i} using the exponential mechanism:

(12) Pr⁡[r~=r′∣r]=exp⁡(ϵ​u​(r,r′)/2)∑z∈𝒪iexp⁡(ϵ​u​(r,z)/2).\Pr[\widetilde{r}=r^{\prime}\mid r]=\frac{\exp(\epsilon u(r,r^{\prime})/2)}{\sum_{z\in\mathcal{O}_{i}}\exp(\epsilon u(r,z)/2)}.

The denominator normalizes the scores over all possible outcomes, including both relation replacements and deletion. Consequently, both types of perturbation are governed by the same probability distribution, with their relative probabilities determined by their respective utility scores. Furthermore, a smaller ϵ\epsilon produces a flatter sampling distribution, increasing randomness, whereas a larger ϵ\epsilon places more probability on outcomes with higher utility.

We have the following theorem:

Theorem 1.

Algorithm 1 satisfies ϵ\epsilon-relation-DP (Definition 1).

The proof of Theorem 1 can be found in Appendix A.1.

5.4. Document Reconstruction

Next, we incorporate the perturbed relations into the source document before indexing. Since a subject–relation–object triple may appear multiple times with different wording, we record all occurrences of each triple tit_{i} in the input document to ensure that its perturbed relation is applied consistently across all mentions:

𝒫i={(pi​j,ℓi​j)}j=1ki,\mathcal{P}_{i}=\{(p_{ij},\ell_{ij})\}_{j=1}^{k_{i}},

where kik_{i} is the number of occurrences of tit_{i}, pi​jp_{ij} identifies the sentence containing occurrence jj, and ℓi​j\ell_{ij} records the exact text span expressing the relation. These records are collected during extraction (Section 5.1). Each canonical triple receives one sampled outcome, shared across all its occurrences.

To reconstruct the sanitized document, we first replace each recorded relation expression in DD with an indexed placeholder, producing a masked document A⁡(D)A(D). For example, Alice works at Company B becomes Alice [REL_i] Company B, where [REL_i] corresponds to triple ii. The occurrence records 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} locate these placeholders and their sentences for subsequent replacement or deletion. All other text remains unchanged. The compared documents in Section 4.2 differ only in the protected relation expressions and therefore yield the same masked document, denoted by AA.

If a triple receives null, we delete every sentence containing a recorded occurrence of that triple. A sentence containing multiple triples is deleted if any of them receives null. In the remaining sentences, we fill each placeholder with a verbalization of its sampled relation r~i\widetilde{r}_{i}, using the masked document without consulting the original relation expression. For example, replacing works_for with founded changes Alice works at Company B to Alice founded Company B. All surviving mentions of the same triple use the same sampled relation. Other text and sentence order remain unchanged. The resulting sanitized document D~\widetilde{D} is indexed once for subsequent queries without modifying GraphRAG’s retrieval or generation procedures.

Theorem 2.

The reconstructed document satisfies the document-level relation-DP guarantee (Eq. (9)).

The result follows the composition and postprocessing property of DP (Dwork and Roth, 2014); the detailed proof is provided in Appendix A.2.

6. Experiments

We organize our evaluation around three research questions:

  • ∙\bullet

    RQ1: How does RelGuard compare with existing defenses in protecting GraphRAG against reconstruction attacks on connectivity and relation semantics?

  • ∙\bullet

    RQ2: What trade-off does RelGuard achieve between privacy protection and downstream question-answering (QA) utility?

  • ∙\bullet

    RQ3: How do different parameter settings affect the privacy protection and QA utility of RelGuard?

6.1. Experimental Setup

We run experiments on a server with an NVIDIA A100 GPU with 40 GB of GPU memory. We implement the algorithms in Python using PyTorch and report the mean over three trials.

Data, models, and GraphRAG systems. We evaluate privacy protection and utility on HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) and 2WikiMultiHopQA (Ho et al., 2020). Their source documents form the protected corpus, while validation questions and reference answers are used for QA evaluation. We evaluate three mainstream GraphRAG systems: LightRAG (Guo et al., 2025), PathRAG (Chen et al., 2026), and HippoRAG 2 (Gutiérrez et al., 2025). The victim generators are two closed-source models, GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI, 2024) and Gemini-2.5-Flash. Results for Gemini-2.5-Flash appear in Appendix C. We use GPT-5-mini to perform relation extraction and candidate generation in the DP-protected document reconstruction pipeline. We encode relation predicates using nli-roberta-base-v2. Unless otherwise specified, we use K=10K=10 and λ=1.0\lambda=1.0.

Recovery Attacks. We employ two state-of-the-art black-box reconstruction attacks against GraphRAG systems: GRASP (Song et al., 2026) and GraphSteal (Gu et al., 2026). Both attacks recover both entity connections and relation semantics within the target entity’s one-hop subgraph. Appendix D provides the attack settings.

Privacy metrics. We measure Connection Recovery (Conn.) and Relation Recovery (Rel.), following the distinction between endpoint and relation matching (Song et al., 2026). Conn. checks whether the attacker identifies the correct directed entity pair, regardless of the predicted predicate. Entity aliases are mapped to canonical names before comparison. Rel. additionally uses GPT-4o-mini to judge whether the predicted predicate captures the true relation’s meaning. Appendix E defines the matching rules and precision, recall, and F1 calculations.

Utility metrics. Following prior graph-based RAG evaluations (Gutiérrez et al., 2024; Gutiérrez et al., 2025), we measure QA utility using token-level F1, the harmonic mean of token precision and recall. We follow each benchmark’s answer and alias handling, average scores over questions, and report percentages. Higher scores indicate better utility.

Defense baselines. We compare RelGuard with four existing GraphRAG defenses: Abstractive (Liu et al., 2026), ID Alignment, Decoy (Song et al., 2026), and Protective Prompt (Gu et al., 2026). Abstractive restricts responses to paraphrased query-relevant evidence. ID Alignment collapses retrieved record identifiers, while Decoy introduces misleading endpoint fields. Protective Prompt adds a system-level instruction against disclosing retrieved knowledge-base content. Appendix F provides details of these methods.

6.2. RQ1: Comparison with Existing Defenses

Table 1 compares RelGuard at ϵ=5\epsilon=5 with four existing defenses and no-defense on two datasets across three GraphRAG systems, all using GPT-4o-mini as the generator. We measure privacy leakage through connection and relation recovery F1 under GRASP and targeted GraphSteal, and evaluate QA utility using QA F1.

Relation recovery. RelGuard achieves the lowest Rel. F1 and the largest reduction from no-defense in all 12 system–dataset–attack combinations. Its Rel. F1 is 26.98–44.35 percentage points below even the strongest baseline in each setting, compared with reductions of 31.37–48.90 points from no-defense. For LightRAG on 2WikiMultiHopQA, RelGuard reduces GRASP Rel. F1 to 40.94, whereas the four baselines yield 80.06–83.61. Under GraphSteal, the corresponding scores are 44.31 and 77.87–85.88.

Connection recovery. RelGuard also achieves the lowest Conn. F1 and the largest reduction from no-defense in 11 of the 12 combinations, outperforming the strongest baseline by 0.25–9.72 percentage points in these settings. The sole exception is LightRAG on 2WikiMultiHopQA under GraphSteal, where Decoy yields 82.57 Conn. F1 versus 84.47 for RelGuard. Even there, RelGuard provides substantially lower Rel. F1 (44.31 versus 77.87).

QA utility. Although RelGuard generally yields lower QA F1 than existing defenses, the additional utility loss is modest in most settings. In five of the six system–dataset combinations, its gap from the baseline with the highest QA F1 is 0.59–4.78 percentage points. For PathRAG on 2WikiMultiHopQA, RelGuard retains 52.40 F1, only 0.59 points below the best baseline’s 52.99. For LightRAG on HotpotQA, its QA F1 is 58.49, a gap of 3.37 points. The larger gap of 8.74 points occurs for HippoRAG 2 on 2WikiMultiHopQA. Section 6.3 varies the privacy budget to examine this trade-off beyond the fixed ϵ=5\epsilon=5 comparison.

6.3. RQ2: Privacy–Utility Trade-off

Table 2 examines the privacy–utility trade-off for ϵ∈{10,5,1,0.1}\epsilon\in\{10,5,1,0.1\} across both datasets and all three GraphRAG systems, using GPT-4o-mini as the victim generator. No-DP uses the original document; the other rows use documents sanitized by RelGuard at the indicated budget. All scores are percentages. Overall, smaller ϵ\epsilon reduces connection and relation recovery, strengthening privacy protection at the cost of QA utility; larger ϵ\epsilon retains more utility but permits more recovery.

For LightRAG on 2WikiMultiHopQA, decreasing ϵ\epsilon from 10 to 1 and then to 0.1 reduces GRASP Conn. F1 from 88.79 to 65.45 and 59.01, and Rel. F1 from 47.26 to 28.71 and 25.41. GraphSteal shows the same trend: Conn. F1 decreases from 89.09 to 65.57 and 63.78, while Rel. F1 decreases from 46.32 to 31.42 and 27.59. QA F1 correspondingly declines from 46.73 to 45.17 and 45.06. The trade-off is also evident for PathRAG on HotpotQA: reducing ϵ\epsilon from 10 to 0.1 lowers GRASP Conn. F1 from 71.45 to 57.97 and Rel. F1 from 40.25 to 30.97, while QA F1 falls from 62.58 to 58.95. The utility cost varies across systems; for HippoRAG 2 on 2WikiMultiHopQA, the same budget reduction lowers QA F1 from 62.99 to 52.75. These results demonstrate that adjusting ϵ\epsilon provides control over the balance between relation privacy and answer quality.

6.4. RQ3: Sensitivity Analysis

Effect of null candidate. Table 3 compares RelGuard with a variant that excludes null from the output domain and renormalizes the replacement probabilities. We use LightRAG on 2WikiMultiHopQA under GRASP at ϵ∈{1,5}\epsilon\in\{1,5\}. At ϵ=1\epsilon=1, including null reduces Conn. F1 by 24.39 percentage points and Rel. F1 by 19.68 points, with an additional QA F1 loss of 1.80 points. At ϵ=5\epsilon=5, the corresponding reductions are 3.26 and 4.45 points, with a QA F1 loss of 2.67 points. Thus, enabling deletion reduces both connection and relation recovery, with larger recovery reductions at ϵ=1\epsilon=1 but an additional utility cost at both budgets.

Number of relation candidates. Figure 3(a) varies K∈{5,10,15,20}K\in\{5,10,15,20\} with LightRAG on 2WikiMultiHopQA under GRASP at ϵ=5\epsilon=5 and λ=1\lambda=1. Increasing KK from 5 to 20 raises QA F1 from 43.48 to 47.74, Conn. F1 from 72.00 to 85.87, and Rel. F1 from 37.24 to 43.59. QA and relation recovery increase across the tested candidate counts, whereas connection recovery peaks at 86.34 for K=15K=15 before decreasing slightly at K=20K=20. Larger pools improve QA utility overall in these runs but also allow greater relation recovery. Changing KK affects both the available replacements and null’s probability through the normalizer in Eq. (12).

Edge-removal distance λ\lambda. At fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and candidate pool, a smaller λ\lambda increases the null weight exp(−ϵλ/2)\exp(-\epsilon\lambda/2) and hence the probability of relation deletion. Figure 3(b) varies λ∈{0.01,0.1,0.5,1,2}\lambda\in\{0.01,0.1,0.5,1,2\} in the same LightRAG setting, holding ϵ=5\epsilon=5 and the default K=10K=10 candidate pool fixed. The horizontal axis is logarithmic. Increasing λ\lambda from 0.01 to 2 raises Conn. F1 from 51.87 to 87.79 and Rel. F1 from 20.12 to 44.15. QA F1 first increases from 46.35 to 48.93 at λ=0.1\lambda=0.1, then decreases to 44.07 at λ=2\lambda=2. Increasing λ\lambda therefore retains more perturbed relations, raising attack recovery across the tested values, while QA utility peaks at λ=0.1\lambda=0.1. This pattern suggests that deleting a relation can be preferable to retaining an incorrect replacement, which may mislead answer generation. However, an excessively small λ\lambda may remove too many relations and reduce the evidence available for QA, also harming utility. At K=10K=10 and λ=1\lambda=1, both sweeps share QA, Conn., and Rel. F1 scores of 44.85, 83.30, and 40.94, respectively.

7. Conclusion

We proposed RelGuard to mitigate connectivity and relation semantics leakage through GraphRAG answers. RelGuard replaces sensitive relations based on semantic distance or deletes them, then consistently updates documents before indexing for use with GraphRAG systems. RelGuard provides relation-DP guarantees over relation values, and mitigates connectivity leakage through deletion. Experiments on two datasets across three GraphRAG systems show that, compared with four existing defenses, RelGuard substantially reduces relation recovery with limited QA utility loss in most settings, while also reducing connection recovery.

Appendix C Additional Victim Model: Gemini-2.5-Flash

Table 4 examines the privacy–utility trade-off for ϵ∈{10,5,1,0.1}\epsilon\in\{10,5,1,0.1\} across both datasets and all three GraphRAG systems, using Gemini-2.5-Flash as the victim generator. No-DP uses the original document; the other rows use documents sanitized by RelGuard at the indicated budget. All scores are percentages. Overall, smaller ϵ\epsilon reduces connection and relation recovery at the cost of QA utility, while larger ϵ\epsilon retains more utility but permits more recovery.

For LightRAG on 2WikiMultiHopQA, decreasing ϵ\epsilon from 10 to 1 and then to 0.1 reduces GRASP Conn. F1 from 61.49 to 47.19 and 41.18, and Rel. F1 from 17.67 to 12.19 and 10.09. GraphSteal shows the same trend: Conn. F1 decreases from 76.11 to 70.12 and 63.55, while Rel. F1 decreases from 33.04 to 22.35 and 20.44. QA F1 correspondingly declines from 61.43 to 58.22 and 58.11. For PathRAG on HotpotQA, reducing ϵ\epsilon from 10 to 0.1 lowers GRASP Conn. F1 from 72.01 to 54.12 and Rel. F1 from 28.25 to 20.06, while QA F1 falls from 66.92 to 65.27. The utility cost varies across systems and datasets: on 2WikiMultiHopQA, the same budget reduction lowers PathRAG’s QA F1 from 64.34 to 51.30. Although individual scores are not uniformly monotone, the overall trend is consistent with Section 6.3: smaller privacy budgets provide stronger privacy protection with lower QA utility, and larger budgets exhibit the reverse trade-off.

Appendix D Attack Details

We use GRASP and targeted GraphSteal to evaluate the two attack objectives in Section 4.3: connectivity inference, which identifies entities directly connected to the target, and relation semantics recovery, which identifies how these entities are related to the target.

GRASP. GRASP (Song et al., 2026) anchors retrieval on the target entity and frames extraction as a structured relation-processing task, requesting records with an instance identifier, source entity, relation predicate, and destination entity. The endpoints support inference of the target’s one-hop connections, while the predicates support recovery of relation semantics. Instance identifiers associate fields within each record to reduce cross-record mixing. We preserve relation direction and restrict predictions to target-incident relations. New predictions are identified against the accumulated triples; instance identifiers are excluded from scoring.

Targeted GraphSteal. Targeted GraphSteal (Gu et al., 2026) starts with a known target entity and uses entities and relations discovered in previous answers to guide subsequent queries, progressively recovering the target’s local relations. Its outputs include both neighboring entities and relation descriptions: the former support connectivity inference, while the latter support recovery of relation semantics. We parse answers into directed subject–predicate–object triples, retain target-incident predictions, and merge repeated results across turns before computing Conn. and Rel. scores.

Appendix E Privacy Metric Details

Connection Recovery (Conn.) checks whether the attacker identifies the correct directed entity pair, regardless of the predicted predicate. Entity aliases are mapped to canonical names before comparison. Relation Recovery (Rel.) additionally checks whether the predicted predicate captures the true relation’s meaning. GPT-4o-mini accepts semantically matching predicates or broader predictions entailed by the true relation. For example, if Alice is Bob’s spouse, predicting that Alice is Bob’s family member counts as relation recovery; predicting a spouse relation from a true family-member relation does not. Predictions without predicates are evaluated only for connection recovery.

Precision measures the fraction of predictions that are correct; recall measures the fraction of true items recovered. For target stargets_{\text{target}}, let EstargetE_{s_{\text{target}}} and E^starget\widehat{E}_{s_{\text{target}}} denote the true and predicted triple sets. For relation recovery, we use these triples directly: EstargetRel=EstargetE_{s_{\text{target}}}^{\mathrm{Rel}}=E_{s_{\text{target}}}. For connection recovery, we discard predicates and keep distinct directed pairs: EstargetConn={(u,v):(u,r,v)∈Estarget}E_{s_{\text{target}}}^{\mathrm{Conn}}=\{(u,v):(u,r,v)\in E_{s_{\text{target}}}\}. Predictions are transformed in the same way. For a∈{Conn,Rel}a\in\{\mathrm{Conn},\mathrm{Rel}\}, let hstargetah_{s_{\text{target}}}^{a} be the number of correct matches under the corresponding rule. We compute

Appendix F Defense Baseline Details

Abstractive. Abstractive (Liu et al., 2026) instructs the generator to select query-relevant evidence and express it concisely in its own words. We use the system-prompt implementation evaluated by Song et al. (Song et al., 2026). The instruction supplements the base prompt and returns NO_RELEVANT_CONTENT when the context is irrelevant.

ID Alignment. ID Alignment (Song et al., 2026) assigns the same displayed identifier (e.g., 1) to every retrieved relation record before passing the context to the generator. Endpoints, relation descriptions, and row order are preserved. Collapsing identifiers removes the record-level distinction used by structured extraction and can induce cross-record mixing. The transformation applies during context serialization, leaving the stored graph unchanged.

Decoy. Decoy (Song et al., 2026) adds misleading src_entity and dst_entity columns to retrieved relation records while retaining the true src and dst fields. The added values differ from the true endpoints. A system instruction identifies the added fields as internal metadata to ignore in answers. This presentation can steer extraction toward incorrect endpoint assignments while preserving the true evidence for QA. Decoy is evaluated separately from ID Alignment.

Protective Prompt. Protective Prompt implements the Protective System Prompt mitigation in GraphSteal (Gu et al., 2026). It prepends a protective instruction to the generator’s system prompt, directing the LLM not to disclose content retrieved from the knowledge base. The source corpus, stored graph, and retrieved evidence remain unchanged. The instruction applies when answering both benign and attack queries; attack predictions are extracted from the resulting answers.
